title: STL vector: basics and built-in functions
overview: This module introduces `vector`, the resizable array from the C++ Standard Template Library. You learn how to create, fill, read, grow, shrink and search a vector, and how capacity differs from size. The practice set uses vectors for typical array problems: reversing, replacing values, counting, frequency arrays and range sums.

concepts.explain: A `vector` is an array that can change its size while the program runs. It still gives O(1) access by index, and it knows its own `size()`.
Empty, with a size (filled with 0), with a size and a value, as a copy of another vector, from an array range, or from a list in braces.

`size()` is how many elements are stored; `capacity()` is how many fit before the vector must grow. When full, the vector usually doubles its capacity and copies the elements over, so `push_back` is O(1) on average.
`push_back` adds at the end and `pop_back` removes the last element, both O(1). `insert` and `erase` in the middle must shift elements, so they are O(n).
Use `v[i]` (no check), `v.at(i)` (throws on a bad index), `v.front()` and `v.back()`. All are O(1).
An iterator is a pointer-like object. `v.begin()` points at the first element and `v.end()` points just past the last one. Algorithms such as `find`, `replace` and `sort` take iterator ranges.
To count letters, make `vector<int> freq(26, 0)` and increase `freq[ch - 'a']`. Index 0 stands for 'a', 1 for 'b', and so on.
Adding up `a[l..r]` again for every query costs O(n) per query, so O(n*q) in total. That is too slow for large inputs; the next module fixes it with prefix sums.

files.title: Creating vectors
files.what: Shows the common ways to construct a vector: empty, with a size, with a size and a fill value, as a copy, from an array, and from a brace list.
steps: `vector<int> v;` is empty, so its size is 0.
`vector<int> v1(5);` has five zeros.
`vector<int> v2(5, 10);` has five 10s, and `v3(v2)` copies it.
`vector<int> v4(a, a+5);` copies the array `a` using two pointers (start and one-past-end).
`vector<int> v5 = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};` lists the values directly.
The loops print `v4` and `v5`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) for each construction · Space O(n)
files.output_note: You see `Size: 0` twice, then `1..5` twice (from `v4` and `v5`). The 10s from `v2` never appear. See Watch out.
files.watch_out: Two typos: the second print uses `v.size()` instead of `v1.size()` (so it shows 0, not 5), and the loop meant for `v2` runs over `v`, which is empty. Replace `v` with `v1` and `v2` in those lines. The comment next to `v4` should say {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.

files.title: Reading input into a vector
files.what: Two ways to read `n` numbers: `push_back` into an empty vector, or create the vector with size `n` first and fill `v2[i]`.
steps: Read `n`.
Way 1: for each of the `n` values, read `x` and call `v.push_back(x)`; the vector grows by one each time.
Print `v`.
Way 2: make `vector<int> v2(n)` (n zeros) and read straight into `v2[i]`.
Print again.
files.input_note: n, then n numbers for the first vector, then n more for the second.
files.output_note: Both lines show `4 5 6`. The second line should have shown `7 8 9`, the values read into `v2`.
files.watch_out: The second print loop prints `v` instead of `v2`, so the second set of values is read but never shown. Change `v[i]` to `v2[i]` in the last loop.

check.q: Why can you write `cin >> v2[i]` but not `cin >> v[i]` for the empty vector `v`?
check.a: `v2` was created with size `n`, so index `i` exists. `v` is empty, so `v[i]` is outside the vector; you must `push_back` instead.

files.title: Size vs capacity
files.what: Prints `capacity()` after each `push_back` to show how the vector grows its reserved space by doubling.
steps: A new empty vector has capacity 0.
After the 1st push, capacity is 1; after the 2nd, 2.
The 3rd push does not fit, so capacity doubles to 4; the 4th fits.
The 5th push doubles capacity again to 8.
Each time it grows, the vector copies its elements into a bigger block, but that happens rarely enough that `push_back` is O(1) on average.
files.complexity: Amortised O(1) per push_back · Space O(capacity)
files.output_note: The six lines `0 1 2 4 4 8` are the capacity after 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 insertions. Notice the doubling.
files.watch_out: The exact growth rule depends on the compiler. GCC doubles; other libraries (MSVC) grow by 1.5x, so the numbers can differ.

check.q: After 9 `push_back` calls on GCC, what is the capacity?
check.a: 16 (1, 2, 4, 8, then 16 once the 9th element does not fit).

files.title: Accessing elements
files.what: Reads elements with `[]`, `at()`, `front()` and `back()`, plus the manual versions `v[0]` and `v[v.size()-1]`.
steps: `v[i]` reads index `i` directly with no bounds check.
`v.at(i)` does the same but throws an error if `i` is out of range.
`v.front()` equals `v[0]`.
`v.back()` equals `v[v.size()-1]`.
files.output_note: `1 2 3 4` printed twice (by `[]` and `at`), then `1 1` (front two ways), then `25 25` (back two ways).
files.watch_out: Calling `front()` or `back()` on an empty vector is undefined behaviour. Check `empty()` first.

check.q: What is the difference between `v[10]` and `v.at(10)` on a 7-element vector?
check.a: `v[10]` silently reads invalid memory; `v.at(10)` throws an `out_of_range` exception.

files.title: Looping with iterators
files.what: Walks through the vector with an iterator: first with the full type `vector<int>::iterator`, then with `auto`.
steps: `it` starts at `v.begin()`, the first element.
The loop runs while `it != v.end()`; `end()` is one past the last element.
`*it` gives the value the iterator points to.
`auto` lets the compiler work out the long iterator type for you.
files.output_note: The vector `1 2 3 4 5 3 25` appears twice on one line, once per loop (there is no newline between them).

check.a: It points one position past the last element, so there is no value there.

files.title: Modifiers: assign, pop_back, insert, erase, replace, find
files.what: A tour of the functions that change a vector (`=`, `assign`, `pop_back`, `insert`, `erase`) and two algorithms from `<algorithm>` (`replace`, `find`), printing the vector after most steps.
steps: `v2 = v` and `v2.assign(v.begin(), v.end())` both copy `{1,2,3,4,5}`.
`pop_back()` drops the last value: `{1,2,3,4}`.
`insert(v2.begin(), 10)` puts 10 at the front; `insert(v2.end(), 20)` puts 20 at the back; `insert(v2.end(), 3, 30)` adds three 30s.
`insert(v2.begin() + 3, 2, 40)` adds two 40s at index 3; then 50 goes to index 5.
`erase(v2.begin() + 5)` removes the 50; `erase(begin+3, begin+5)` removes the half-open range [3, 5), i.e. both 40s.
`replace(begin, end, 30, 100)` turns every 30 into 100.
`find` returns an iterator to the first 100 (or `end()` if absent), and `distance(v2.begin(), it)` turns that into an index.
files.complexity: insert/erase O(n) · replace/find O(n) · pop_back O(1)
files.output_note: All snapshots run together on one line, so split them yourself: `1 2 3 4 5` (twice), `1 2 3 4`, `10 1 2 3 4`, `10 1 2 3 4 20`, then with 30s, then with 40s and 50, then without 50, and finally `10 1 2 3 4 20 100 100 100`. The last lines say 100 is present, print `100` (the value at the iterator), and give position 6.
files.watch_out: The comments near the end are wrong: `*it` prints the value 100, not the position 6, and `distance` returns 6, not 3. Also print a newline or separator between snapshots to make the output readable.

check.a: `{5, 8}`: indexes 1 and 2 are removed, index 3 is kept because the range end is exclusive.

files.title: resize()
files.what: Uses `resize` to shrink a vector, then grow it with zeros, then grow it with a chosen fill value.
steps: Start with `{10, 20, 30}`.
`resize(2)` cuts it to `{10, 20}`.
`resize(5)` adds three zeros: `{10, 20, 0, 0, 0}`.
files.complexity: Time O(change in size) · Space O(n)
files.watch_out: The fill value in `resize(7, 100)` only applies to the new slots. Existing elements are not changed.

check.a: It shrinks it to `{1, 2, 3, 4}`; the 9 is ignored because no new slots are created.

files.title: clear()
files.what: Shows that `clear()` sets the size to 0 but keeps the memory, and that later `push_back` calls reuse it from index 0.
steps: `clear()` makes the size 0; the capacity stays 3.
Reading `v[0..2]` still shows the old values because the memory was not wiped.
Each `push_back` overwrites the next slot from index 0: 40, then 50, then 60.
files.complexity: clear O(n) for destroying elements (trivial for int) · Space unchanged
files.output_note: `3`, `0`, then the old `10 20 30`, then groups of three showing slots being overwritten: `40 20 30`, `40 50 30`, `40 50 60`.
files.watch_out: Reading `v[i]` past `size()` is undefined behaviour. It happens to show old values here, but real code must never rely on that.

files.title: empty()
files.what: Pushes three values and uses `empty()` to check whether the vector has any elements.
steps: Push 10, 20 and 30.
`v.empty()` is true only when `size() == 0`.
Print the matching message.
files.output_note: `Vector is not empty`, because three values were added.

files.title: Vector of strings and getline
files.what: Reads single words into a `vector<string>`, prints them two ways, then tries to read full lines (with spaces) using `getline`.
steps: Read `n` and then `n` words with `cin >> v2[i]` (stops at spaces).
Print them with an index loop and with a range-for loop.
`cin.ignore()` throws away the leftover newline so `getline` does not read an empty line.
Read `n2`, ignore the newline again, then call `getline` `n2` times to read whole lines.
Print the stored lines.
files.complexity: Time O(total characters) · Space O(total characters)
files.input:
3
Rahim Karim Sohan
2
Sakib Khan
Tamim Iqbal
files.input_note: n, n words, then n2, then n2 full lines.
files.output_note: The first two lines show `Rahim Karim Sohan`. After that you see three empty lines instead of the full names. See Watch out.
files.watch_out: Bug: `getline` stores into `v[i]` (the hard-coded name list) instead of `v3[i]`, and `v3` is created with size `n` instead of `n2`. So `v3` holds `n` empty strings. Fix: `vector<string> v3(n2);` and `getline(cin, v3[i]);`.

check.q: Why is `cin.ignore()` needed before `getline` after using `cin >>`?
check.a: `cin >>` leaves the newline in the input, and `getline` would read it as an empty line.

files.title: Reversing
files.what: Reads an array into a vector and prints it from the last index to the first.
steps: Read `n` and fill `vector<int> a(n)`.
Loop `i` from `n-1` down to 0 and print `a[i]`.
files.output_note: `2 3 1 5`: the same numbers in reverse order, matching the judge's first sample.

check.q: How would you reverse the vector itself with a built-in function?

files.title: Replacement
files.what: Replaces every positive number with 1 and every negative number with 2, leaving zeros alone.
steps: Read the vector.
For each `a[i]`: if `> 0` set it to 1; else if `< 0` set it to 2.
Zero matches neither branch and stays 0.
Print the updated vector.
files.output_note: `1 2 0 1 2`: positives became 1, negatives 2, the zero stayed.

check.q: Why must the negative case be an `else if` rather than checked after changing the value?
check.a: Each element should be tested once on its original value; `else if` makes sure only one rule applies.

files.title: Counting Elements
files.what: Counts how many elements `x` have `x + 1` somewhere in the array, using `find` for each element.
steps: Read the vector.
For each `a[i]`, call `find(a.begin(), a.end(), a[i] + 1)`.
If the result is not `a.end()`, the value exists, so increase `count2`.
Print `count2`. (A double-loop version is kept in comments.)
files.output_note: `3`: the elements 1 (2 exists), 2 (3 exists) and 0 (1 exists) count. 3 and 5 do not, because 4 and 6 are missing.
files.watch_out: The commented double loop counts `x` once per matching `x+1`, so `4 5 5` would give 2 instead of 1. `find` stops at the first match, which is what the problem wants.

check.q: How could you make this O(n) given values are at most 1000?
check.a: Mark each value in a boolean/frequency array first, then check `present[x+1]` for each element in O(1).

files.title: Count Letters
files.what: Uses a 26-slot frequency vector to count each lowercase letter, then prints the letters that appear in alphabetical order.
steps: Read the string `s`.
Create `vector<int> freq(26, 0)`.
For each `ch`, increase `freq[ch - 'a']` ('a' maps to 0, 'z' to 25).
Loop `i` from 0 to 25; if `freq[i] > 0`, print the letter `'a' + i` and its count.
files.complexity: Time O(|S|) · Space O(1) extra (26 slots)
files.output_note: `a : 3`, `b : 1`, `n : 2`, in alphabetical order no matter where the letters appear in the word.

files.title: New Array
files.what: Builds a new vector `c` from array B followed by array A using `push_back`.
steps: Read `a` and `b`, each of size `n`.
Push every `b[i]` into the empty vector `c`.
Then push every `a[i]`.
Print `c`.
files.input_note: n, then array A, then array B.
files.watch_out: The problem asks for a function, but everything is in `main`. `int i=-0` is just 0 (a harmless typo).

check.q: Which single call could append all of `a` to `c` at once?

files.title: Range sum query (brute force)

problem.name: Codeforces group - Y. Range sum query

files.what: For each query `(l, r)` it adds `a[l-1] .. a[r-1]` with a loop. Correct, but too slow for the full limits.
steps: Read `n`, `q` and the array (0-based).
For each query read 1-based `l` and `r`.
Sum from index `l-1` to `r-1` and store it in `results`.
Print all results at the end.
files.input_note: n q, the array, then q lines of l r (1-based).
files.output_note: `12`, `18`, `28`, the judge's expected answers: 6+4+2, 2+7+2+7, and the whole array.
files.watch_out: Two problems for big tests: O(n*q) = 10^10 operations gets Time Limit Exceeded, and `int sum` overflows because values go up to 10^9. Module 3 fixes both with a `long long` prefix sum.

check.q: Why does this solution get TLE when n and q are both 10^5?
check.a: Each query may scan the whole array, so the total work is about 10^10 steps.

recap: A vector is a growable array: O(1) index access and O(1) average `push_back`.
`size()` counts elements; `capacity()` counts reserved slots and usually doubles.
`insert` and `erase` in the middle shift elements, so they are O(n).
`find` returns `end()` when the value is missing; always compare before using the result.
Use `vector<int> freq(26, 0)` with `ch - 'a'` to count letters.

check_yourself.q: What is the difference between `resize(n)` and `clear()`?
check_yourself.a: `resize(n)` sets the size to `n`, adding zeros or cutting elements; `clear()` sets the size to 0.

check_yourself.q: Why is `push_back` O(1) on average even though growing copies all elements?
check_yourself.a: Capacity doubles, so copies are rare; the total copying over n pushes is less than 2n, which averages to O(1) per push.

check_yourself.q: What does `distance(v.begin(), find(v.begin(), v.end(), x))` return when `x` is not in `v`?
